MUJAHID:v2p455#2/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p455#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p455#2/r1.claim: Mujahid says night and day are alternating black and white.

MUJAHID:v2p455#2/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p455#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p455#2/r2.claim: Mujahid says gratitude means thanking one's Lord for His blessing.

MUQATIL:25:61-66/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:25:61-66/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:25:61-66/r2.claim: Night and day alternate, so one can replace the other for someone occupied with a need and provide time for remembrance or gratitude through worship.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p488/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p488/r3.speaker: الحسن
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p488/r3.claim: Al-Hasan says night and day alternate to give someone who fell short at night another opportunity during the day, and vice versa.

FARRA:v2p271/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p271/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p271/r1.claim: يتذكر in Ubayy's reading supports the doubled reading يذكر; the lighter reading of Abdullah, Hamza, and many others means the same, as shown by another verse's variant.

MAJAZ:v2p79/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p79/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p79/r5.claim: Khilfah means night comes after day and day after night, each taking the other's place.

MAJAZ:v2p79/r6.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p79/r6.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p79/r6.claim: Khilfah is a verbal noun, so its form is the same for singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine subjects.

MAJAZ:v2p79/r7.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p79/r7.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p79/r7.claim: The poems use khilfah for alternation or succession.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p71/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p71/r1.speaker: الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p71/r1.claim: Hasan explains night and day succeeding each other: what someone misses in one can be made up in the other.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p71/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p71/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p71/r2.claim: The Prophet says envy is justified only for one given wealth that he spends day and night and one given the Quran that he recites day and night.

TAB-FULL:v17p485/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r1.claim: One view takes “alternating” to mean each time period replaces the other, allowing missed worship in one to be made up in the other.

TAB-FULL:v17p485/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r2.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r2.claim: ʿUmar tells someone who missed a night prayer to make it up during the day, citing God's making night and day alternate.

TAB-FULL:v17p485/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says what a person misses at night can be done in the day, and what is missed by day can be done at night.

TAB-FULL:v17p485/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r4.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r4.claim: Al-Hasan similarly says either period can make up what a person missed in the other.

TAB-FULL:v17p485/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r5.claim: Another view, reported from Mujahid, takes night and day as contrasting black and white.

TAB-FULL:v17p485/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r6.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v17p485/r6.claim: A further view from Mujahid says each period succeeds the other: when one departs, the other arrives.

TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r1.claim: The alternation of night and day is a sign for whoever wants to recall God's command and turn to truth, or give thanks for the blessing of their succession.

TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r2.claim: Mujahid says gratitude means thanking one's Lord for the blessing of both night and day; their alternation is a sign.

TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r3.claim: Most Medinan and Basran readers and some Kufans double the consonant in “remember”; most Kufans read it without doubling.

TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p488#2/r4.claim: The doubled and undoubled readings are established and close in meaning, so either is correct.

TAB-FULL:v17p488/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r1.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd says the contrast between night and day lets people know when to fast or pray; “alternation” means one departs and the other comes.

TAB-FULL:v17p488/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r2.claim: “Khilfa” is a singular verbal noun serving as the predicate for night and day; in Arabic a successor replaces something that has passed.

TAB-FULL:v17p488/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r3.claim: An unnamed poet's line uses “khilfa” for animals replacing one another after the ants have eaten the gathered food.

TAB-FULL:v17p488/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r4.speaker: زهير
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r4.claim: Zuhayr's line has gazelles walking in succession, one group taking the place of another.

TAB-FULL:v17p488/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p488/r5.claim: The poet may instead mean that the gazelles differ in color or form, or that their movement alternates between going and coming.

ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r1.speaker: الحسن
ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r1.claim: Al-Hasan says night or day offers another chance for remembrance and gratitude if the other period was missed.

ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r2.claim: Linguists explain خلفة as one period following another; Zuhayr's word خلفة witnesses this use.

ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p74/r3.claim: Another interpretation takes the periods as alternating opposites, supported by the verse on creation and alternation of night and day.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r1.claim: Night preceded day: when the joined heavens were considered, there was only darkness between them.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r2.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r2.claim: The Jews asked the Prophet about Friday, and he said God created its night and day in two hours of it.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r3.claim: A report from Uzayr describes God's creation before night and day: his throne was over water, darkness, and air, angels bore it, and God opened the treasury of light and path of darkness so night and day alternated by his command.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r4.claim: “Alternating night and day” means white and black.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r5.claim: Night's darkness follows the daylight's brightness.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r6.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r6.claim: Night and day differ as black and white; a believer who forgets at one time can remember at the other.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r7.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2717#2/r7.claim: Umar lengthened the forenoon prayer to complete a portion he had left, citing the verse about night and day as an opportunity to remember and give thanks.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r1.claim: Night makes up for what someone missed doing during the day, and day makes up for what was missed at night.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r2.claim: Night follows day and day follows night so a person who fell short in worship can make it up.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r3.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r3.claim: Whoever cannot act by day may act at night, and whoever cannot act at night may act by day; each replaces the other.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r4.claim: Someone unable to act at night gets another opportunity in the day, and someone unable by day gets one at night.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r5.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r5.claim: Take from the night what you can; if you miss something in the day, make it up at night.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r6.claim: Night and day each succeed the other.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r7.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن اسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2718/r7.claim: Alternation makes worship possible: with only night people could not know how to fast, and with only day they could not know how to pray; each replaces the other for God's servants.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r1.claim: The phrase “for whoever wants to remember” is described as a sign for that person.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r2.speaker: الضحاك
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r2.claim: “Whoever wants to remember” means whoever wants to take admonition.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r3.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r3.claim: “Or wants to give thanks” means giving thanks for the blessing God granted through night and day.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r4.speaker: الضحاك
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2719/r4.claim: “Or wants to give thanks” means obedience.

NAHHAS:v3p165/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p165/r8.speaker: المدنيون وأبو عمرو وعاصم والكسائي
NAHHAS:v3p165/r8.claim: They read yadhakkar, from yatadhakkar with tāʾ assimilated into dāl, meaning to remember and reflect on creation.

NAHHAS:v3p165/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p165/r9.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p165/r9.claim: The alternate yadhkur reading means that a person can recognize these signs by remembering them.

SULAMI:v2p66#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p66#2/r1.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p66#2/r1.claim: Night and day succeed one another for whoever wishes to serve and worship God.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r10.claim: Remembering means praying night prayer in daytime and daytime prayer at night.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r11.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r11.claim: Gratitude is voluntary prayer after obligatory prayer; the verse is also said revealed about Umar.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r6.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب والحسن
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r6.claim: Night and day alternate so one can make up worship missed in the other.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r7.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r7.claim: They alternate as opposites, one white and the other black.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r8.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r8.claim: Each succeeds the other as one departs and the next arrives.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r9.speaker: زهير
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p153/r9.claim: A poem uses khalfa of animals succeeding one another in movement.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r1.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r1.claim: The intensive reading يذكر means to reflect and think until one recognizes God's power and infers His oneness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r2.speaker: حمزة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r2.claim: Hamza reads the verb lightly, meaning to recall in one part of the day what was forgotten during the other part.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r3.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r3.claim: A further possibility is that the two periods are times for remembering God's transcendence and praising Him, as 33:41 commands.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r4.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r4.claim: Al-Farra says يذكر and يتذكر can mean the same; the Companion reading in 2:63 uses يتذكروا for the usual اذكروا.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r5.claim: Night and day succeeding one another provide evidence of God's power and an opportunity to remember and obey Him.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r6.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r6.claim: The exegetes also take the alternation of day and night as a chance to remember and obey God.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r7.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p570/r7.claim: On Mujahid's view, remembrance here is reflection and inference about God's power, rather than verbal praise and glorification.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r1.claim: شكور is another verbal noun of شكر, alongside شكرا, and the author points to 76:9 for its usage.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns a person who wants to take heed and obey God.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r3.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p571/r3.claim: Mujahid says the person thanks his Lord for the blessing He gives in both periods.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:25:61-63/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:25:61-63/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:25:61-63/r2.claim: Night and day replace one another, so missed night worship can be made up in daytime; remembrance includes prayer, glorification, and recitation, and gratitude means thanking and obeying God.

JISHUMI:v7p5320/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5320/r2.speaker: حمزة
JISHUMI:v7p5320/r2.claim: Hamza reads يذكر with a light, still ذال; others use the doubled form.

JISHUMI:v7p5320/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5320/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5320/r9.claim: Khilfatan means alternating or succeeding one another.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r3.claim: Night and day replace one another, letting a person make up worship missed in one during the other.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r4.speaker: شقيق
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r4.claim: A man told ʿUmar that he missed the night prayer; ʿUmar told him to make it up in the day.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r5.claim: Night and day differ as black and white.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r6.claim: They replace each other in cycles of light and darkness and increase and decrease.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r7.claim: Ḥamza reads يذكر with lighter consonants; the others read يتذكر with doubling, meaning reflect and take heed; Mujāhid says gratitude is for God’s blessing in both.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r8.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p92#2/r8.claim: “Or seek gratitude” means thanking the Lord for His blessing in both periods.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p217#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p217#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p217#2/r8.claim: Khilfa means that night and day succeed one another, each replacing the other.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p218/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p218/r1.speaker: زهير
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p218/r1.claim: Zuhayr's cited line illustrates the changing night and day by depicting every creature moving slowly and seeking its prey.

TABRISI:25:61-62/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:25:61-62/r5.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
TABRISI:25:61-62/r5.claim: Khilfah means each period succeeds the other, allowing someone who missed a night act to make it up by day and vice versa; this explanation is reported from Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Hasan.

TABRISI:25:61-62/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:25:61-62/r6.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:25:61-62/r6.claim: A report from Abu Abd Allah says to make up daytime prayer at night and nighttime prayer during the day.

TABRISI:25:61-62/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:25:61-62/r7.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:25:61-62/r7.claim: Mujahid instead explains night and day as opposites, one black and the other white.

TABRISI:25:61-62/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:25:61-62/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:25:61-62/r8.claim: Remembering means reflecting that a manager and controller unlike either night or day must exist, and turning worship to Him; gratitude can mean thanking God for His blessings in both periods.

TABRISI:25:61-62/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:25:61-62/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:25:61-62/r9.claim: On the first interpretation, gratitude refers to voluntary worship after completing the obligatory prayer.

TABRISI:25:61-70#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:25:61-70#2/r6.speaker: أبو عبيدة
TABRISI:25:61-70#2/r6.claim: Khilfah means that each thing follows another: night succeeds day, and day succeeds night; Zuhayr’s verse witnesses this sense.

RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r10.speaker: أنس بن مالك
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r10.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet told Umar to make up missed nighttime voluntary prayer in the day and missed daytime prayer at night.

RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r11.speaker: مجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r11.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Kisaʾi take khilfah to mean that night and day differ, like black and white or long and short; al-Razi prefers the first view.

RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r12.claim: Al-Razi considers the succession-and-compensation interpretation of khilfah more likely.

RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r8.claim: One meaning of khilfah is that night and day succeed one another, each providing an opportunity to make up work missed in the other.

RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v24p92#2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas says that an act missed during either night or day can be made up during its counterpart.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r1.claim: Night has great merit: the Prophet was commanded to pray at night, believers are praised for rising from their beds, and a report praises late prayer, a time when supplications are answered, and the Lord’s descent.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r2.speaker: حمزة
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r2.claim: Hamza, as well as Ibn Waththab, Talha, and al-Nakhaʿi, reads yadhkur with a still dhāl and ḍamma on kaf; the Ubay codex adds a tāʾ, and the remaining readers use a doubled kaf, all with similar meaning.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r3.claim: The lightened reading may mean recalling in one time what was missed in the other, or remembering God’s transcendence and praising Him during both periods.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r4.claim: Shukūr is an intensive verbal noun meaning the same as shukr, like kufūr and kufr; the cycles of night and day sustain people’s livelihood and prompt gratitude.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62#2/r5.claim: The close connects the signs to the question “what is the Merciful?”: He is the One able to make these things.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r1.speaker: أبو عبيدة
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r1.claim: Abu Ubayda defines khilfa as one thing following another, as night and day each succeed the other; the word can describe alternating bodily positions or new plant leaves.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r10.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r10.claim: Ibn al-Arabi quotes Dhu al-Shahid al-Akbar: people’s created completeness is life and knowledge, but sleep, bodily needs, and physical deficiency afflict them; a person should reduce sleep through restraint and worship where possible.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r11.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r11.claim: Ibn al-Arabi calculates that a sixty-year life spent sleeping half the night and a sixth of the day wastes two thirds, leaving twenty years, and calls it folly to spend that much life in fleeting pleasure rather than lasting worship.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r12.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r12.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says things do not differ in rank by themselves but by qualities; which is superior, night or day, is disputed, with fasting enough to indicate the answer.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r2.speaker: زهير بن أبي سلمى
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r2.claim: Zuhayr’s verse uses khilfa for successive groups of gazelles and their young appearing from hiding places.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r3.claim: A second poem illustrates a woman who shifts seasonally between her winter and summer homes, with successive settings described as khilfa.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r4.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r4.claim: Mujahid understands khilfa as opposition or difference, such as white and black; the author says the succession meaning is stronger.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r5.claim: Other interpretations are alternation in light and darkness and in increase and decrease, or an omitted phrase meaning that night and day possess difference.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r6.claim: The alternation lets people remember and reflect that God did not create it in vain, and thank Him using their reason, thought, and understanding.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r7.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس والحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r7.claim: They explain the verse as allowing anyone who missed a good deed by night to make it up by day, and anyone who missed one by day to make it up by night.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r8.claim: A sound report says that a person whose customary night prayer is overtaken by sleep may pray after sunrise before noon and receive the night prayer’s reward, with the sleep counted as charity.

QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r9.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:25:62/r9.claim: Muslim reports Umar from the Prophet: whoever sleeps through his regular nightly portion may read it between dawn and noon and receive the reward as if reading at night.

BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r1.claim: Night and day alternate, each replacing the other in what one should do; this resembles the Quran's statement that they succeed one another.

BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r2.claim: Alternation lets people reflect on God's favors and craftsmanship and recognize a wise, necessary Creator, or make up worship missed in one period during the other.

BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r3.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
BAYDAWI-FULL:25:62-63/r3.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read يذكر with a form meaning remember or reflect.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r1.claim: Night and day succeed one another, or each can compensate for worship missed during its counterpart.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r2.claim: The Ḥamza and Khalaf reading may mean remembering God or remembering what was missed and making it up.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p175#2/r3.claim: Their alternating hours enable reflection on the One who governs them and gratitude for His favor.

QASHANI:25:61-63/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:25:61-63/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:25:61-63/r2.claim: The alternation of ego-darkness and heart-light lets the seeker remember the forgotten primordial covenant and reflect on meanings and realities.

QASHANI:25:61-63/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:25:61-63/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:25:61-63/r3.claim: Night is an opportunity for gratitude through worship and the acquisition of virtues and moral habits.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p124/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p124/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p124/r6.claim: Khilfah is parsed as a verbal noun or a noun of state used circumstantially: night and day each succeed and follow the other; Arabic also uses it for frequent back-and-forth, as in cited poetry.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r1.claim: Another gloss makes khilfah mean increase and decrease; Mujāhid, Qatāda, and al-Kisāʾī describe alternating darkness and brightness or long and short days.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r2.speaker: عمر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r2.claim: ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥasan say that anyone who misses good or prayer in one part of the cycle can make it up in the next.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r3.claim: Mujāhid and others understand remembrance as reflecting on created things and thanking God for intellect and understanding.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reports Ubayy b. Kaʿb's “yadhdhakkara” reading and says night and day reveal a powerful changer; rest at night and activity by day are blessings and opportunities to make up missed worship, as 28:73 explains.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r5.speaker: النخعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p125/r5.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Waththāb, Zayd b. ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, and Ḥamza read “tadhakkara” with the light form of the verb.

SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r1.claim: خلفة may be the second object of جعل or a circumstantial, depending on the parse of جعل.

SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r2.claim: خلفة may be a verbal noun for one thing replacing another, a noun of manner, or a form from alternation; poetry by al-Matarun and Zuhayr witnesses these uses.

SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r3.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r3.claim: Abu al-Baqa explains the singular خلفة as one of night and day replacing the other, a relation requiring both.

SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:25:62/r4.claim: الشكور with ḍamma is the verbal noun gratitude; with fatḥa it is an intensive adjective.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p120#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p120#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p120#2/r2.claim: Night and day succeed one another continuously: when one goes, the other arrives, as also described in 14:33, 7:54, and 36:40.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r1.claim: Their alternation times worship: a person who misses a devotional portion at night can make it up by day, or vice versa; a sound hadith also describes God's nightly and daytime acceptance of repentance.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r2.claim: ʿUmar lengthened his Duḥā prayer to complete or make up his regular portion, citing this verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says missed worship at night may be performed in the day, and missed daytime worship at night; ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and al-Ḥasan agree.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r4.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p121/r4.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda explain khilfatan as differing in character: one is dark and the other bright.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r1.claim: Night, whose sign is the moon, and day, whose sign is the sun, succeed one another with opposite qualities and replace one another in many functions, allowing what is missed in one to be made up in the other.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r2.speaker: ابن جرير
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r2.claim: Ibn Jarir says the Arabs use khalaf and khilfa for alternating opposites, such as light and darkness or heat and cold.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r3.speaker: الرازي
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r3.claim: Al-Razi in al-Lawamiʿ explains khilfa as things taking turns, each succeeding its companion, or as people who differ.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r4.claim: The majority's doubled reading yadhdhakkara points to reflection through reason: change on this scale requires a powerful, choosing changer and can bring even a disbeliever to faith.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r5.speaker: حمزة
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r5.claim: Hamza's light reading yadhkura means remembrance; the signs of divine power and knowledge are so clear that a slight attention suffices without extended reflection.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p333/r6.claim: The alternating cycles invite believers to give profound thanks: each night or day arrives before the previous one's benefits are lost, while perpetual light or darkness would produce fatigue and disrupt timed duties.

DURR-FULL:v6p269/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p269/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p269/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses night and day as black and white; he also says one can make up an act missed at night during the day, or vice versa.

DURR-FULL:v6p269/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p269/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v6p269/r5.claim: Mujahid says night and day succeed each other so people can remember God’s favors and give thanks; believers may also make up missed remembrance during the other period.

DURR-FULL:v6p269/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p269/r6.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v6p269/r6.claim: Umar lengthened his forenoon prayer to complete a missed regular portion, citing the alternation of night and day; Saʿid ibn Jubayr also says either period substitutes for the other to make up worship.

DURR-FULL:v6p271/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p271/r1.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v6p271/r1.claim: Al-Hasan says worship that cannot be done at night can be done by day, and each period lets a person make amends for what he could not do in the other.

DURR-FULL:v6p271/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p271/r2.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v6p271/r2.claim: Salman advises a man unable to pray at night to keep up worship by day; Qatada reports a nightly hour when a Muslim’s prayer for good is granted and urges good works because day and night carry people toward their lifespans and Resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v6p271/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p271/r3.speaker: عاصم
DURR-FULL:v6p271/r3.claim: ʿĀṣim recited yadhakkara with a doubled consonant; Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi is also reported to recite this form.

BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r1.claim: Because خلفة is a verbal noun, the construction needs an omitted noun; night and day succeed one another, allowing missed optional worship to be made up in the other period.

BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r2.speaker: النبي عليه السلام
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r2.claim: The Prophet told Umar that a missed night recitation can be made up in daytime and a missed daytime recitation at night.

BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r3.claim: Alternatively, night and day alternate so people can count years and time, and have set periods for earning a livelihood and for rest.

BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p173#2/r4.claim: The alternation recalls God's blessings and alerts people to His perfect wisdom and power.

BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r1.claim: Remembering means reflecting on God's favors and creation to recognize the wise, necessary, merciful Creator; this is directed to unbelievers, while gratitude is directed to believers.

BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r2.claim: شكورا with damma is a verbal noun for thanking God through obedience; أو may also mean and, making night and day occasions for remembering and thanking.

BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r3.claim: The use of أو emphasizes that either remembrance or gratitude independently fulfills the purpose; coordination with و might imply both are required together.

BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r4.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r4.claim: Al-Raghib defines gratitude as recognizing and showing a favor, contrasts it with concealing blessings, and describes gratitude of heart, tongue, and limbs.

BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r5.claim: An optional litany is not legally obligatory to make up, but doing so is recommended: regular litany brings regular spiritual influx and connection, like a river supplied by mountain rain and snow.

BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r6.speaker: الصائب
BURSEVI:v6p173#3/r6.claim: Sa'ib's couplet says a weak stream cannot reach the sea, illustrating why worshippers replace missed litanies to keep their spiritual supply flowing; the author urges morning and evening practice and warns against neglect.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r1.claim: Khilfah may mean night and day alternate, each replacing the other in appropriate activities; this is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r10.claim: Remembering may figuratively mean making up missed worship; Majmaʿ al-Bayān also says voluntary prayer after obligatory prayer.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r11.claim: Another good reading is reflection on God’s creative signs and gratitude for blessings in night and day; the author says it nearly eclipses alternatives absent transmitted views.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r12.claim: The lām may attach to ‘made’ or express purpose; aw distributes the senses or permits either independently, while the longer wording emphasizes remembrance.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r13.speaker: أبي بن كعب
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r13.claim: Ubayy reads an yatadhakkara, the original form before tāʾ changes to dhāl and assimilates.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r14.speaker: النخعي وابن وثاب وزيد بن علي وطلحة وحمزة
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r14.claim: These readers use yadhkura, the form-II imperfect meaning ‘remember.’

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r2.claim: Alternatively, one succeeds and follows the other; khilfah names the resulting state.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r3.claim: Some read khilfah as difference in length or darkness and brightness, the latter attributed to Mujāhid; it may encompass both and other contrasts.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r4.speaker: البحر وزهير
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r4.claim: Al-Baḥr cites an idiom for frequent trips to relieve oneself; Zuhayr’s verse about animals following behind illustrates repeated succession.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r5.claim: A second poet depicts a woman moving between winter and summer homes, illustrating repeated alternation.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r6.speaker: القاموس
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r6.claim: Al-Qāmūs defines khalf and khilfah as mutually different; this needs no omitted ‘possessing alternation,’ since singular names the difference.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r7.claim: Another reading is that each of night and day frequently comes and goes.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r8.claim: Alternation lets one make up a devotional portion missed in one period during the other; early authorities transmit this sense.

ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r9.speaker: عمر
ALUSI-FULL:v19p42#2/r9.claim: Al-Ṭayālisī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim report that ʿUmar prolonged forenoon prayer to complete a missed litany and recited the verse.

ELMALILI:25:62/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:25:62/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:25:62/r1.claim: Khilfah means either that night and day succeed one another, or that one replaces what could not be done during the other.

ELMALILI:25:62/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:25:62/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:25:62/r2.claim: The verse addresses people who want to reflect, make up deficiencies, or undertake intellectual or practical work.

ELMALILI:25:62/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:25:62/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:25:62/r3.claim: For idle people who have no intention to think or fulfill duties, changes in time have no meaning; they try to kill time.

ELMALILI:25:62/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:25:62/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:25:62/r4.claim: Reflection means considering signs of mercy and proofs of craftsmanship to recognize one's own shortcomings and the Wise Creator's power and mercy.

ELMALILI:25:62/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:25:62/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:25:62/r5.claim: Gratitude means fulfilling the duty of worship owed to the All-Merciful.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r1.claim: The imperfect yadhdhakkar indicates repeated renewal of remembrance, while the verbal noun shukūr suggests gratitude can occur at once; arāda is repeated because the two forms do not coordinate smoothly.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r2.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r2.claim: The majority read yadhdhakkar with a doubled open dhāl, from yata-dhakkaru by assimilation of tāʾ into dhāl.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r3.speaker: حمزة وخلف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v19p66/r3.claim: Ḥamzah and Khalaf read yadhkur with a still dhāl and rounded kāf; it has the same meaning, though the doubled form implies greater effort, and both acts suit night and day.

TABATABAI:25:41-62/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:25:41-62/r6.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
TABATABAI:25:41-62/r6.claim: Al-Faqih transmits al-Sadiq's instruction to make up what was missed at night during the day and what was missed by day at night, citing the alternating night and day.

TABATABAI:25:62/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:25:62/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:25:62/r2.claim: Khilfa means something that replaces another; night and day succeed one another and each can serve for remembrance or gratitude when the other has passed.

TABATABAI:25:62/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:25:62/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:25:62/r3.claim: Remembrance means returning to innate proofs of God's unity and attributes, culminating in faith; gratitude is speech or action praising His gifts, including worship and good works.

TABATABAI:25:62/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:25:62/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:25:62/r4.claim: Alternating night and day is a favor: one may recover faith, worship, or a good deed missed during one period in the other.

TABATABAI:25:62/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:25:62/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:25:62/r5.claim: The verse links back to the sun and moon: though the arrogant are kept from ascending to God's presence, servants can still approach and receive guidance by alternating daylight and moonlit night.

TABATABAI:25:62/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:25:62/r6.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:25:62/r6.claim: Some interpret remembrance as the obligatory prayer and gratitude as the voluntary prayer; al-Tabataba'i says the verse can fit this reading but does not require it.

ASAD-NOTES:25:61#n49/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:25:61#n49/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:25:61#n49/r1.claim: The particle aw here adds an explanation, equivalent to in other words, rather than presenting an alternative.

ASAD-NOTES:25:intro/r4.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:25:intro/r4.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:25:intro/r4.claim: Revelation belongs to the same majestic creative order as nature; the Prophet's complaint that followers discarded the Qur'an is especially relevant today.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p356/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p356/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p356/r4.claim: Verses 61-77 teach that the world's nights and days suffice as reminders for anyone willing to remember and give thanks; the humble servants of God contrast with the arrogant Quraysh, who are warned of consequences for disregarding God's favor.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p390/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p390/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p390/r1.claim: Reminder addresses the intellect and gratitude the heart; signs throughout creation sustain both, but benefiting from them depends on intention, which God tests without coercing human choice.

QIRAAT-ER:25:62:13#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:25:62:13#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:25:62:13#1/r1.claim: Form I describes simple remembering rather than Form V's intensive self-reflection.

STUDYQURAN:25:62/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r1.speaker: R, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r1.claim: Some say night and day alternate so worship or good deeds missed in one can be accomplished during the other.

STUDYQURAN:25:62/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r2.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r2.claim: Ibn Kathīr cites a ḥadīth in which God extends His Hand by night to forgive daytime sin and by day to forgive nighttime sin.

STUDYQURAN:25:62/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r3.speaker: Q, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r3.claim: Some understand khilfah as opposition: night and day are opposites, one dark and the other light.

STUDYQURAN:25:62/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r4.claim: The alternation of night and day is a Quranic sign of God, as is the passage of day into night and night into day.

STUDYQURAN:25:62/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r5.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:25:62/r5.claim: The verse concerns reflecting on or giving thanks for the blessings of day and night.

STUDYQURAN:25:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:25:intro/r3.speaker: A minority
STUDYQURAN:25:intro/r3.claim: A minority classifies most of the surah as Madinan but verses 68–70 as Makkan.
